You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details:
- Symptom from the issue report: parsing a 0-sized “ux” (X7875 New Unix) local extra field throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at X7875_NewUnix.parseFromLocalFileData. The index in the exception (e.g., 13) matches the position where the method tries to read the first byte of the extra field, even though the provided length is 0.
- Test context: X7875_NewUnixTest.testParseReparse exercises parsing and re-emitting various valid encodings, including the “minimal” 3-byte case with zero-length UID/GID: ZERO_LEN = {1, 0, 0}. It also reparses the data produced by the writer, which for zero values is the 5-byte sequence {1, 1, 0, 1, 0} (the test explicitly asserts that the writer never emits zero-length entries).
- Problem in implementation:
  - X7875_NewUnix.parseFromLocalFileData(byte[] data, int offset, int length) unconditionally reads from the byte array:
    - It reads version = data[offset++], then uidSize = data[offset++] (lines 208–210).
    - It then copies uidSize bytes, updates offset, and reads gidSize = data[offset++] (lines 211–218).
    - It finally copies gidSize bytes (lines 216–218).
  - The method never consults or validates the length parameter; there are no checks that at least 3 bytes are available for version/uidSize/gidSize, nor that enough bytes remain for uidSize and gidSize.
  - As a result, when the local extra field is truly empty (length == 0) or shorter than declared, the code attempts to read data[offset], leading to ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of a controlled ZipException. This directly explains the real-world failure observed by Tika when encountering a 0-sized “ux” local entry.
- Why the test exposes the issue:
  - While the test’s ZERO_LEN case supplies the minimal 3-byte header and thus doesn’t crash, the test later reparses data produced by getLocalFileDataData() and also invokes parseFromCentralDirectoryData with an empty array. The parser’s lack of bounds checks on the input means any legitimately empty or too-short extra field will cause an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException rather than a graceful return or a ZipException. The same underlying flaw (ignoring the length parameter and missing boundary checks) affects both local and potentially central directory parsing.
- Summary:
  - Root cause: parseFromLocalFileData ignores the provided length and performs unchecked reads, assuming at least 3 bytes and then uidSize/gidSize bytes exist. This causes ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException for 0-sized or truncated “ux” extra fields.
  - Expected behavior: If length == 0, the parser should not read at all (treat as absent/empty field) and leave UID/GID unchanged (or reset predictably), or at worst throw a ZipException with a clear message. If length < 3 or if remaining bytes are insufficient for uidSize/gidSize, the method should validate and throw ZipException instead of accessing the array out of bounds.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
